paragraphs.heading: Waiting for the first success
paragraphs.text: The geometric distribution answers a waiting question. You run an endless sequence of Bernoulli trials that are independent and identically distributed, and you ask when the first success will occur. The name comes from the fact that its probabilities form a geometric sequence, and it is also sometimes called the Furry distribution.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways of counting
paragraphs.text: There are two versions, and its probability formula depends on which one you pick. One version, X, counts the trials needed, k = 1, 2, 3, …, giving P(X = k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹p, where p is the chance of success on each trial. The other, Y = X − 1, counts the failures before the first success, so its values start at 0. These two should not be confused, so it is wise to say which one you mean by stating its possible values.

paragraphs.heading: Rolling until a 1
paragraphs.text: Suppose you roll a six-sided die until a 1 comes up. Each roll is independent and has a 1/6 chance of success, so the number of rolls you need follows a geometric distribution with p = 1/6. For X, the expected value is E (X) = 1/p. Here that means an average of 1/(1/6) = 6 rolls, and an average of (1 − 1/6)/(1/6) = 5 failures before the 1 shows up.

paragraphs.heading: No memory
paragraphs.text: Among discrete probability distributions, the geometric one is the only memoryless one. In plain terms, the failures you have already had do not change how many more trials you will need before a success. The same property appears in the exponential distribution, and the geometric distribution is its discrete version. Going the other way, the exponential distribution is the matching continuous distribution.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and spread
paragraphs.text: The variance of X is var (X) = (1 − p)/p², and switching to Y changes the mean to (1 − p)/p but leaves the variance the same. Its excess kurtosis never drops to zero or below, which makes it what statisticians call leptokurtic. Put simply, its tail carries more weight and dies away more slowly than a Gaussian's. As p gets smaller, the entropy grows, which reflects more uncertainty when success is rare.
